chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Safwan ibn Yahya, and Ibn Abi Umayr, from Jamil, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:
A camel for two camels, and an animal for two animals, hand to hand (immediate exchange), there is no problem with it.

key_terms.الْبَعِيرُ: A camel (specifically a female camel used for riding/breeding, often used generically for camel)
key_terms.لَيْسَ بِهِ بَأْسٌ: There is no problem with it (it is permissible)
key_terms.يَداً بِيَدٍ: Hand to hand (immediate exchange without delay)

ai.seo_question: Can I trade one camel for two camels in Islam?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the specific application of riba al-fadl to livestock, distinguishing them from the 'six items' (gold, silver, wheat, barley, dates, salt) by allowing unequal quantities in immediate exchange. Shia jurists utilize this narration to establish that the strict equality requirement applies primarily to staple commodities and currency, while animals are governed by the condition of hand-to-hand possession (qabd) to prevent uncertainty (gharar). This ruling underscores the practical flexibility in pre-modern trade, ensuring that transactions involving livestock remain free from usury despite varying counts.
